name: Priya Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach oboe on Tuesdays, play junior parts with a chamber group and record short lines for local adverts. I finished secondary school and still ask the lead player for help when a passage runs fast.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part do you like, and what feels hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like hearing a pupil make a reed speak for the first time. The hard part is a chamber booking that moves after my partner and I have arranged the children’s pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the chamber players that AI sorting the booking email is fine. The audience still expects an oboe to breathe through the opening line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have nine months of expenses saved and my partner’s postal supervisor pay is steady. One cancelled recital would not put the mortgage in danger, though I would miss the fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will keep Tuesday oboe pupils and the chamber group’s Saturday rehearsals this season. I sometimes use AI to tidy a programme note, but I read every word before sending it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the bills. There are several other ensembles nearby if this one loses a date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when the recital hall closed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A recital was cancelled last spring when the hall roof leaked. I would ask the organiser for a half-fee cancellation clause next time rather than argue at the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your daughter see you do before playing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My daughter hears me scrape a reed every morning. A good oboe sound starts with slow work, not a polished poster.

I would ask for a **cancellation fee** before the next recital.
think: Our **nine-month cushion** and postal income protect the mortgage from one lost date.
I would still miss the **recital fee** if a hall closed.
do: Keep **Tuesday oboe pupils** and Saturday chamber rehearsals this season.

feel: I feel **calm** about bills and available nearby ensembles.

fieldNote: Her **strong reserve** and partner income explain calm despite occasional cancellations.

steps.text: Keep Tuesday oboe pupils and Saturday chamber rehearsals

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the chamber group that AI could book halls, check scores and make cheap demo tracks, so our contracts should state live fees clearly. I would ask our organiser for paid rehearsal dates in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My short oboe tracks for local adverts could lose buyers, about a fifth of a busy month. Our cushion makes a search possible. The lost advert income is still ours to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would ask the organiser for three months of paid rehearsals and look at two nearby ensembles’ posted auditions. In the first year I would try the music library’s score-checking tool only after its librarian demonstrates it, use a score without pupil names, and play every changed note before trusting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about losing advert income. I can still choose among nearby auditions if paid calls fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the score-checking trial safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not buy a subscription for a trial. If the tool changes an oboe range incorrectly or sends pupil material outside the library, I would stop and use my paper part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you audition for any nearby ensemble?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would audition only if a seat is actually posted, paid and I can play its excerpts. I will not miss the children’s pickup for an informal promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the chamber group that AGI by 2028 could write its scores, but a live oboe still needs a player. I would ask the organiser for a signed season calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the advert tracks to vanish in 2028, and booking software may reduce paid rehearsals. Robots for hands-on playing follow around 2031, so the chair has longer than the tracks, but it is not guaranteed forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would collect my advert invoices and ask the organiser for signed dates. If 2028 AGI cuts chamber rehearsals, I would audition for a posted paid oboe chair only if my excerpts are ready and school pickup fits, while keeping Tuesday pupils until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about losing the tracks and some rehearsals, but nine months saved gives us room to search. I would not tell the children we are moving on the strength of an audition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you compare before accepting a distant chair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep six months of expenses untouched. If the only post is farther away, I would compare the written net pay after travel with current earnings before accepting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your partner cover pickup for that job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask my partner to cover one audition-day pickup, not every week. A new oboe chair has to fit our school routine after the audition too.

I would defend the **paid oboe chair** while live work remains.

steps.text: Audition for posted paid oboe chair if 2028 rehearsals fall, excerpts ready and pickup fits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the chamber group that AGI by 2031 gives us five years to teach younger players and keep live rehearsals worth paying for. I would ask for a paid reed workshop rather than free demonstrations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The advert tracks may end in 2031, but I could earn more teaching beginners and helping them make reeds. Robots around 2034 may play an oboe line, though I do not know who would pay to watch that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This autumn I would price a four-week reed workshop at the community hall, only if six families prepay and the room is available after child pickup. If it fills, I would run it with my beginner lessons; in the first year after 2031 I would keep the workshop only while it covers materials and the hall fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious until the workshop has paid places. Five years lets me test a reed workshop without betting the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many paid places cover the reed materials?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Six families at 15 cover reeds and hall rent and leave me a fee. If only three sign up, I would cancel the next block and keep one-to-one pupils.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach in that workshop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show a child how to scrape a reed without rushing. I would not sell a machine-cut reed as something I made by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children that AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to learn a craft and a way to earn. I would keep teaching oboe while pupils book lessons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 a paid reed workshop could replace advert tracks if enough families return. Robots around 2039 could play onstage, but our current lessons, partner pay and savings protect the next few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this year I would save half of each paid advert fee until our reserve reaches twelve months, after the mortgage and food are covered. In the first year after 2036 I would compare lesson and chamber pay with the prior year and audition for a posted paid seat only if both shrink, excerpts are ready and pickup fits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel uneasy about stage work much later. Our household pay and nine months saved make the near years secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is twelve months already in the bank?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The twelve months are a target, not what is in the account now. If adverts stop early, I would save from lessons only after bills and keep six months untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about a paid promise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children that a steady hand and a paid promise matter. A glossy programme cannot make a mortgage payment.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because advert tracks could go before chamber dates are signed. A written season, posted paid auditions and a workshop with prepaid places would give us routes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what a child learns by making a reed. My oboe pupil hears the reed change before reading the mark on the page.

headlineQuote: My oboe pupil hears the reed change before reading the mark on the page.
portrait: At **43**, Priya is a junior oboist with secondary school education, two children, a mortgage and nine months saved.
Her partner’s **postal pay** steadies household bills while advert and chamber fees remain exposed.
She uses **AI occasionally**, testing a new library tool only with demonstration, nameless parts and manual checks.
She builds a **paid reed workshop** only after six prepayments cover materials and hall costs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end advert tracks before Priya knows whether chamber rehearsals stay paid.
whatWouldHelp: A **written season**, posted paid auditions and a prepaid reed workshop would give Priya options.
